levels.sigmoid.title: Build sigmoid
levels.sigmoid.description:
Build 
$$sigmoid(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(−x))$$
 using the available components.
levels.derivative.title: Differentiate a function
levels.derivative.description:
Build the derivative of $x × exp(x)$: 
$$exp(x) × (1 + x)$$
.
levels.xor.title: Learn XOR
levels.xor.description:
XOR is 1 when two inputs differ and 0 when they match. A straight boundary cannot separate it; use a hidden layer with an activation. Reach loss below 0.05 and 100% accuracy; grading uses training samples, not a separate test set.
This level: input $x$ [4,2] holds the four binary pairs; output $y$ [4,2] gives class 0 and class 1 probabilities per row.

home.titleC: build all the way to GPT.
home.lead: Each level asks you to wire existing parts into a new one, which then joins your library. Sigmoid and softmax first, then backpropagation, optimizers and attention, and finally a GPT you train in the browser and that writes text.
chapter.0.desc: add, mul, exp, log → sigmoid, tanh
chapter.1.desc: Build derivative circuits, then let them calculate how to adjust parameters.
chapter.2.desc: Broadcasting, Matrix multiply, Softmax, Layer normalization
chapter.3.desc: A neural network is a learnable function: input → linear layer → activation → prediction; loss trains shared parameters.
chapter.4.desc: Number characters, turn them into vectors, then predict the next character. Training changes parameters; generation only uses them.
chapter.5.desc: Let positions find and mix relevant content, then use it to predict the next character.
chapter.6.desc: Stack information exchange and per-position processing into a GPT-style character predictor: train against known answers, then generate one character at a time.

levels.0-1.title: Negate
levels.0-1.description:
Negation turns an increase into a decrease.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=−x$, its sign reversed. A scalar is one number.
levels.0-2.title: Subtract
levels.0-2.description:
Subtraction measures a difference.
This level: input scalars $a$ and $b$; output their difference, scalar $y=a−b$.
levels.0-3.title: Reciprocal
levels.0-3.description:
Reciprocals turn division into a product.
This level: input positive scalar $x$; output reciprocal scalar $y=1/x$. Tests use positive numbers.
levels.0-4.title: Divide
levels.0-4.description:
Division compares quantities as a ratio.
This level: input scalar $a$ and positive scalar $b$; output quotient scalar $y=a/b$.
levels.0-5.title: Sigmoid
levels.0-5.description:
Networks need nonlinear functions to model curved relationships.
Sigmoid maps real numbers into (0, 1).
This level: input scalar $x$; output activation scalar $y=σ(x)=1/(1+e⁻ˣ)$.
levels.0-6.title: Hyperbolic tangent
levels.0-6.description:
Tanh centers activation.
This level: scalar $x$ in; activation scalar $y=tanh(x)=(eˣ−e⁻ˣ)/(eˣ+e⁻ˣ)$ out.
levels.0-7.title: ReLU
levels.0-7.description:
Maximum returns the larger of two numbers.
This level: input scalar $x$; output activation scalar $y=max(x,0)$: negative values become zero; others stay unchanged.
levels.0-8.title: Square root
levels.0-8.description: This level: scalar $x>0$ in; root scalar $y=√x$ out.
levels.1-1.title: Derivative of a square
levels.1-1.description:
A derivative is the slope at an input, not the function value.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=f′(x)$ for $f(x)=x²$.
levels.1-2.title: Product rule
levels.1-2.description:
A product depends on both factors.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=f′(x)$, the slope of $f(x)=x·eˣ$.
levels.1-3.title: Chain rule
levels.1-3.description:
Nested functions pass changes through each layer.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=f′(x)$, the slope of $f(x)=e³ˣ$.
levels.1-4.title: Derivative of log
levels.1-4.description: This level: scalar $x>0$ → scalar slope $(log x)′$.
levels.1-5.title: Derivative of sigmoid
levels.1-5.description:
This derivative will pass changes back to the input during training.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=σ′(x)$, the rate of change of the Sigmoid function $f(x)=σ(x)$.
levels.1-6.title: Derivative of tanh
levels.1-6.description:
Learn this derivative to prepare for training networks.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=tanh′(x)$, the rate of change of $f(x)=tanh(x)$.
levels.1-7.title: Log chain rule
levels.1-7.description:
Apply the chain rule to a logarithm containing a square.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=f′(x)$, the slope of $f(x)=log(1+x²)$.

errors.matmul_shape: Matrix multiply shapes do not fit: a is {a}, b is {b}. The last axis of a must equal the second-to-last axis of b.
levels.xor.hint1: Use a hidden layer to form nonlinear features, then a second layer for class probabilities. Linear layers alone cannot separate XOR.
levels.xor.hint2: Use random weights [2,8], [8,2], biases [8], [2]; Sigmoid between layers, Softmax last.
levels.0-1.hint1: Negation turns an increase into a decrease. What multiplier reverses the sign of $x$? For example, 3 becomes −3.
levels.0-1.hint2: Set Constant to −1, feed it and $x$ into Multiply, then connect the result to $y$. Edit the constant in Attributes.
levels.0-2.hint1: Subtraction measures errors or gaps. Subtracting a number means adding its what? For example, $5−2=3$.
levels.0-2.hint2: Feed $b$ into Negate, then feed its result and $a$ into Add. Connect the result to $y$.
levels.0-3.hint1: Reciprocals turn division into multiplication. The natural logarithm obeys $log(1/x)=−log(x)$; its base is the constant $e≈2.718$.
levels.0-3.hint2: Connect Logarithm → Negate → Exponential. Exponential undoes the natural logarithm: $exp(log(x))=x$, where $exp(u)=eᵘ$. For example, 2 has reciprocal 0.5.
levels.0-4.hint1: Division computes ratios. Dividing by $b$ means multiplying by its what? $a$ may be negative, so do not take its logarithm.
levels.0-4.hint2: Feed $b$ into Reciprocal, then multiply its result by $a$ using Multiply. For $a=−6$ and $b=2$, $y=−3$.
levels.0-5.hint1: $σ$ denotes Sigmoid; $e$ is the base of natural exponentials. Activations let networks express nonlinear relationships. Start with the innermost $−x$.
levels.0-5.hint2: Use Negate, then Exponential; Add the constant 1 and finish with Reciprocal. At $x=0$, $y=0.5$.
levels.0-6.hint1: Tanh, the hyperbolic tangent, maps reals into (−1, 1), a zero-centered activation. $e$ is the natural exponential base. Try multiplying numerator and denominator by $eˣ$.
levels.0-6.hint2: Use Multiply and Exponential to get $u=e²ˣ$, then Subtract, Add and Divide for $(u−1)/(u+1)$. Reuse the output of $u$ with multiple wires. At $x=0$, $y=0$.
levels.0-7.hint1: ReLU is an activation that keeps positive values. What should you compare $x$ with to remove negative values?
levels.0-7.hint2: Feed $x$ and a Constant set to 0 into Maximum. For example, −2 becomes 0, while 3 stays 3.
levels.0-8.hint1: A square root restores the units of a squared quantity. $√x$ is the positive square root, or $x$ to the power ½; for example, $√9=3$.
levels.0-8.hint2: The natural logarithm turns powers into multiplication: $√x=exp(0.5·log(x))$. Connect Logarithm, Multiply by a Constant of 0.5, then Exponential.
levels.1-1.hint1: $f$ denotes a function; a prime $′$ means its derivative with respect to the input. The power rule is $(xⁿ)′=n·xⁿ⁻¹$, with fixed exponent $n$.
levels.1-1.hint2: Use Multiply with $x$ and a Constant of 2. At $x=3$, the function value is 9, but the required slope is 6.
levels.1-2.hint1: Product rule: $(u·v)′=u′·v+u·v′$, where $u$ and $v$ are functions of $x$. Here $u=x$ and $v=eˣ$; $e$ is the natural exponential base.
levels.1-2.hint2: The derivatives of $x$ and $eˣ$ are 1 and $eˣ$. Factor to get $eˣ·(1+x)$ using Exponential, Add and Multiply. At $x=0$, output 1.
levels.1-3.hint1: The chain rule handles nested functions: multiply the outer derivative, evaluated at the inner value, by the inner derivative. Here the inner value is $u=3x$ and the outer function is $eᵘ$; $e$ is the natural exponential base.
levels.1-3.hint2: The outer derivative is $eᵘ$ and the inner derivative is 3. Multiply $x$ by 3, apply Exponential, then Multiply by 3. At $x=0$, output 3.
levels.1-4.hint1: $log$ is the natural logarithm; the prime means differentiate with respect to $x$. Logarithms compress numeric ranges. If $u=log(x)$, then $x=eᵘ$. Try differentiating both sides.
levels.1-4.hint2: From $1=eᵘ·u′$, obtain $u′=1/x$. Feed $x$ into Reciprocal; at $x=2$, the slope is 0.5.
levels.1-5.hint1: $σ$ denotes Sigmoid and $σ′$ its derivative, used to pass rates of change back to the input. Differentiate $σ(x)=(1+e⁻ˣ)⁻¹$ by the chain rule, then rewrite using $σ(x)$ alone.
levels.1-5.hint2: $σ′(x)=σ(x)·(1−σ(x))$. Use Sigmoid once, then Subtract and Multiply; at $x=0$, output 0.25. Passing unlocks the Sigmoid derivative part.
levels.1-6.hint1: $tanh$ is the hyperbolic tangent; the prime denotes its derivative, used to pass rates of change to a preceding layer. Write it as numerator $u$ over denominator $v$ and use $(u/v)′=(u′v−uv′)/v²$.
levels.1-6.hint2: $tanh′(x)=1−tanh(x)²$. Use Tanh once, Multiply its output by itself, then Subtract from 1. At $x=0$, output 1. Passing unlocks Tanh derivative.
levels.1-7.hint1: $log$ is the natural logarithm. Since $1+x²$ is always positive, $x$ may have either sign. The outer $log(u)$ has derivative $1/u$; the inner value is $u=1+x²$.
levels.1-7.hint2: The inner derivative is $2x$, giving $2x/(1+x²)$. Build it with Multiply, Add and Divide. At $x=1$, output 1.

levels.axes.title: Shapes and axes
levels.axes.description:
Tensors arrange numbers in a shape: [] is one number, [6] a list, [2,3] two rows of three. Each direction is an axis, numbered from 0; −1 always means the last axis, −2 the one before. Summing an axis combines numbers along it. Shapes appear beside node titles; hover for values.
This level: input $x$ [2,3] holds two rows; output $y$ [2] holds their row totals.
levels.axes.hint1: Summing along an axis removes that axis: [2,3] summed along axis 0 gives [3] (one total per column); along axis −1 it gives [2] (one per row).
levels.axes.hint2: Set Sum’s axis to −1. With “Keep dimensions” on, the summed axis stays as length 1 and you get [2,1]; turn it off here.
levels.2-2.title: Broadcasting
levels.2-2.description:
Broadcasting combines different shapes entry by entry. Align from the last axis: lengths must match or one must be 1; missing leading axes count as 1. A length-1 axis reuses its value.
This level: scale rows, then add column offsets: inputs are data $x$ [4,3], row scales $s$ [4,1], column biases $b$ [3]; output $y = x × s + b$ [4,3].
levels.2-2.hint1: No new part needed. Broadcasting is built into add and multiply.
levels.2-6.title: Transpose, then multiply
levels.2-6.description:
Compare two sets of row vectors by pairing every row with every row of the other set. Transpose swaps the last two axes; $bᵀ$ means transposed $b$, leaving batch axes unchanged.
This level: inputs $a$ [4,3], $b$ [5,3] hold row vectors; output $y = a·bᵀ$ [4,5] holds pairwise dot products.
levels.2-6.hint1: Turn $b$ into [3×5], then use the matrix multiplication you built.
levels.2-6.hint2: Use Transpose with axes [−2,−1] into Matrix multiply’s $b$ port; wire $a$ to its $a$ port.
levels.2-1.title: Dot product
levels.2-1.description:
A dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up, useful for weighted scores. Tests also use shorter vectors.
This level: input vectors $a$, $b$ are both [6]; output $y$ [] is their dot product, one number.
levels.2-1.hint1: Wire $a$ and $b$ straight into a multiply. You still get a list of 6.
levels.2-1.hint2: Sum along axis −1 with “Keep dimensions” off: the vector’s only axis is summed away, leaving a single number of shape [].
levels.2-3.title: Mean
levels.2-3.description:
A mean summarizes a row by dividing its sum by its count. Reduce only the last axis and keep it. Tests also use [3,5] and [2,3,4], so do not hard-code division by 6. Passing unlocks Dimension size.
This level: input data $x$ [4,6]; output $y$ [4,1] holds row means.
levels.2-3.hint1: Sum adds up a row. What if every number in the row were 1?
levels.2-3.hint2:
$$x × 0 + 1$$
 is a tensor of ones shaped like $x$. Sum both (keeping dimensions) and divide.
levels.2-4.title: Outer product
levels.2-4.description:
An outer product lists every pairwise product, not just matching positions. Row $i$, column $j$ contains $aᵢ × bⱼ$, where $i$ and $j$ index the two lists. Insert length-1 axes so broadcasting can build the table.
This level: input vectors $a$ [4], $b$ [3]; output $y$ [4,3] holds all pairwise products.
levels.2-4.hint1: Insert dimension adds a length-1 axis where you choose. Stand $a$ up as a column and lay $b$ down as a row.
levels.2-4.hint2: Insert at axis −1 for $a$ and axis 0 for $b$, then multiply.
levels.2-5.title: Matrix multiplication
levels.2-5.description:
Matrix multiplication computes many dot products: result row $i$, column $j$ pairs row $i$ of the left matrix with column $j$ of the right. Broadcast to form entrywise products, then sum the shared-length axis. Tests add a batch axis, so count axes from the end.
This level: inputs are left matrix $a$ [4,3], right matrix $b$ [3,5]; output $y$ [4,5] is their matrix product.
levels.2-5.hint1: Aim for a [4×3×5] block of products: $a$ becomes [4×3×1] and $b$ becomes [1×3×5].
levels.2-5.hint2: Insert at axis −1 for $a$ and axis −3 for $b$. Multiply, then sum over axis −2 without keeping it.
levels.2-7.title: Softmax
levels.2-7.description:
Softmax converts scores to positive probabilities summing to 1 per row: exponentiate, then divide by the row total. Avoid overflow.
This level: input scores $x$ [4,6]; output probabilities $y$ [4,6], each row summing to 1. Computers store numbers with finite precision: this number format cannot hold a value as large as $e^{100}$. Mathematically equal formulas may differ in computational reliability.
levels.2-7.hint1: Subtracting the same constant from a whole row doesn't change Softmax. Which constant is safest?
levels.2-7.hint2: Subtract Reduce maximum on the last axis, keeping dimensions. Apply Exponential; divide by its last-axis Sum, keeping dimensions.
levels.2-8.title: Layer norm
levels.2-8.description:
Layer normalization stabilizes later calculations; it does not produce probabilities. Subtract each row’s mean, then divide by the square root of its variance plus stabilizer $ε = 0.00001$. Constant rows become zero.
This level: input features $x$ [4,8]; output normalized features $y$ [4,8].
levels.2-8.hint1: Variance is the mean of the squared distance from the mean. Epsilon avoids division by zero on constant rows; this component has no extra trainable scale or bias.
ui.tensorProbeHelp: Tensor inputs are read-only. Switch cases to see other data. Hover a node for its full values.
levels.1-8.title: Partial derivatives
levels.1-8.description:
With several inputs, isolate the effect of changing just one.
This level: input scalars $a$, $b$; output scalar $y=∂f/∂a$ for $f(a,b)=a·b+exp(a)$, the rate of change as only $a$ varies. Hold $b$ fixed.
levels.1-8.hint1: $∂f/∂a$ is a partial derivative: it isolates the effect of one input changing. $exp(a)=eᵃ$ is the natural exponential. If $b$ stays fixed, what is the slope of $a·b$?
levels.1-8.hint2: The derivative of $a·b$ with respect to $a$ is $b$; the exponential is its own derivative. Use Exponential and Add for $b+exp(a)$. At $a=0$, $b=2$, output 3.
levels.1-9.title: Another direction
levels.1-9.description:
Practise holding one input fixed while differentiating with respect to another.
This level: input scalars $a$, $b$; output scalar $y=∂f/∂b$ for $f(a,b)=a·exp(a·b)$, the rate of change as only $b$ varies. Hold $a$ fixed.
levels.1-9.hint1: $∂f/∂b$ measures change as only $b$ varies; $exp(u)=eᵘ$. The partial derivatives form the gradient; when nonzero, it points in the direction of steepest local increase. Keep the outer $a$ fixed: what is the derivative of the inner $a·b$ with respect to $b$?
levels.1-9.hint2: One $a$ comes from outside and another from the chain rule. Use Multiply and Exponential for $a²·exp(a·b)$. At $a=2$, $b=0$, output 4.
levels.1-10.title: Backpropagation by hand
levels.1-10.description:
To train a weight, first measure its effect on the output. Weight $w$ scales feature $x$; bias $b$ shifts the baseline. The intermediate value $z=w·x+b$ passes through Sigmoid to give neuron output $f=σ(z)$.
This level: inputs $w$, $x$ and $b$ are scalars. Output scalar $y=∂f/∂w$: the rate of change with respect to the weight, holding $x$ and $b$ fixed.
levels.1-10.hint1: $σ$ is Sigmoid and $z$ is the value before activation. Here there is a single path: multiplying its derivatives back from the output is backpropagation. Use the Sigmoid derivative part from 1-5 for the derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$, then consider the derivative of $z$ with respect to $w$.
levels.1-10.hint2: Use Multiply and Add for $z$, feed it into Sigmoid derivative, then Multiply by $x$: $σ′(w·x+b)·x$. At $w=b=0$, $x=2$, output 0.5. Passing unlocks autodiff and the expression box.
errors.backward_unsupported: Cannot build a derivative graph for “{component}” yet. Build it from supported basic operations instead.
backward.rule.max: Larger operand wins; ties go to a
ui.broadcastHelp: The shapes differ: aligned from the last axis, length-1 or missing axes are copied to fill, then the op runs entry by entry.
gradView.title: Gradient graph
gradView.intro: On top is your circuit; values flow left to right. Below is the mirror the engine draws from it: gradients start at the output and flow right to left, multiplied at each part by that part's own derivative (written on the wire). A value used several times receives several gradients, added at a "+". That is automatic differentiation, the same thing you built by hand in 1-10.
gradView.parameters.initial: On training levels the gradient is taken with respect to the parameters θ (what training changes), not the data. These are the parameters before training; open it again after training to see gradients at the current parameters.
gradView.parameters.current: On training levels the gradient is taken with respect to the parameters θ (what training changes), not the data. These are the parameters you just trained.
gradView.trainingData: Values come from one batch of this level's training data.
gradView.attachedLoss: On this level the engine computes the loss after your output: it compares the probabilities with the right answers using cross entropy. That part is drawn too (labelled "cross entropy"), so the gradient starts at loss. It is only drawn for you to see; your circuit is unchanged.
gradView.openHint: See how the engine derives gradients from this graph
gradView.revealButton: See how the engine does it
gradView.revealIntro: This is the neuron you just did, f = σ(w·x + b). On top, the forward pass. Below, the backward pass the engine generates: start at f and multiply by each local derivative on the way back. It is exactly your σ′(w·x + b)·x; from now on the engine does it for you.
levels.3-1.title: One step downhill
levels.3-1.description:
Training brings predictions closer to targets. Weight $w$ times input $x$ predicts target $t$; loss $L = (w·x − t)²$ measures error, with smaller being better. The gradient $∂L/∂w$ measures how loss changes with weight. A small step against it can reduce loss. Build one update with step size 0.1.
This level: inputs are weight $w$, data $x$, target $t$, all []; output $y = w − 0.1·∂L/∂w$ [] is the updated weight.
levels.3-1.hint1: Chain rule for $∂L/∂w$: a square on the outside, $w·x − t$ inside.
levels.3-1.hint2: $∂L/∂w = 2(w·x − t)·x$. Multiply by 0.1 and subtract it from $w$.
levels.3-2.title: The gradient is a list
levels.3-2.description:
Each weight needs its own update direction. The prediction is dot product $w·x$, with loss $L = (w·x − t)²$. The loss’s rate of change when only one weight changes is a partial derivative. Collect these into the gradient $∂L/∂w$. Output the gradient, not updated weights; tests also use length 5.
This level: inputs are weights $w$ [3], features $x$ [3], target $t$ []; output $y$ [3] holds each weight’s loss gradient.
levels.3-2.hint1: Write $∂L/∂w₁$ first: it differs from the last level's $∂L/∂w$ only by a subscript. Then look at $∂L/∂w₂$ and $∂L/∂w₃$. Which part is the same in all three?
levels.3-2.hint2: $2(w·x − t)$ is one number; multiply it by the whole of $x$. Broadcasting spreads it out.
levels.3-3.title: Mean squared error
levels.3-3.description:
Mean squared error (MSE) measures prediction error: square differences, then average only the last axis, keeping it at length 1. It does not average all axes; a [2,4] test produces [2,1]. Passing unlocks Mean squared error.
This level: inputs are predictions $p$ [8], targets $t$ [8]; output $y$ [1] is the mean of their eight squared errors.
levels.3-3.hint1: Square each error, then average the last axis.
levels.3-3.hint2: Square differences; use Mean, keeping the last axis.
levels.3-4.title: Let it run
levels.3-4.description:
Fit a line to 16 points. Weight $w$ controls slope and bias $b$ the intercept, giving prediction $p = w·x + b$. Store them in two zero-initialized Parameter nodes of shape []. Feed predictions and targets into Mean squared error, then output loss.
The engine repeats forward calculation, backward gradients and parameter updates. Tune the learning rate to reach loss below 0.05 in 60 steps. Grading uses training samples, with no separate test set.
This level: inputs are horizontal coordinates $x$ [16], target vertical coordinates $t$ [16]; output loss [1] is batch mean squared error, not a scalar of shape [].
levels.3-4.hint1: Build a line prediction, then compare it with targets using Mean squared error. Weights and bias must use Parameter; training does not change ordinary inputs or constants.
levels.3-4.hint2: Set two Parameter shapes to []. Multiply $x$ by $w$, add $b$, then feed this and $t$ to Mean squared error → loss. Try rate 0.1–0.5.
levels.train_diverged: Getting further away: the learning rate is too large, and every step overshoots the valley. Lower it.
levels.train_slow: All 60 steps used and loss is still {loss}. Steps too small? Try a larger learning rate.
ui.stepHelp: Take one step: watch values flow forward, gradients flow back and the parameters move.
ui.gradHelp: Gradient of the loss with respect to this value, ∂loss/∂(·)
ui.stepPhase.forward: ① Forward: data flows through the network, loss = {loss}
ui.stepPhase.backward: ② Backward: the gradient flows back from loss; each node gets ∂loss/∂(·)
ui.stepPhase.update: ③ Update: every parameter θ ← θ − η·∂loss/∂θ
levels.3-5.title: Cross entropy
levels.3-5.description:
Cross entropy rewards probability assigned to the correct class. $p$ holds class probabilities; $t$ is one-hot: 1 for the correct class, 0 elsewhere. Compute $−Σ t·log p$ per row (Σ sums classes), then average rows. Lower correct-class probability incurs a larger penalty. Tests change row and class counts.
This level: inputs are probabilities $p$ and labels $t$, both [4,3], one row per sample and column per class; output $y$ [1] is batch cross entropy.
levels.3-5.hint1: One-hot labels select the correct class. Find its negative log probability per sample, then average.
levels.3-5.hint2: Apply Logarithm to $p$, Multiply by $t$, then Sum axis −1 without keeping dimensions. Apply Mean to the resulting [4], then Negate to get [1]. For $t$ = [0,1,0], only the second class’s log probability remains.
levels.neuron.title: One neuron
levels.neuron.description:
A neuron combines features into one score: dot features $x$ with weights $w$, then add bias $b$, giving $y = x·w + b$. Weights control each feature’s influence; bias shifts the score. Here they are supplied inputs, not trained. Processing several rows together is a batch.
This level: inputs are features $x$ [2], weights $w$ [2], bias $b$ []; output score $y$ []. Tests also use $x$ [5,2], giving [5], one score per point.
levels.neuron.hint1: Chapter 2’s dot product sums along the last axis; then add $b$ with an adder.
levels.neuron.hint2: For $x$ [5×2], the dot product sums along the last axis (each point’s two coordinates), giving one number per row; $b$ broadcasts across those 5 numbers. Don’t sum along the first axis (the point index).
levels.layer.title: A layer
levels.layer.description:
A layer lets several neurons score every point at once. Put their weights in columns of matrix $W$ (input port $w$), with biases in vector $b$. Then $y = xW + b$ computes all scores; each row of $x$ is a point. Passing unlocks Linear layer.
This level: inputs are features $x$ [4,2], weights $w$ [2,3], biases $b$ [3]; output scores $y$ [4,3], one row per point and column per neuron.
levels.layer.hint1: $x$ [points×coords] times $W$ [coords×neurons] gives [points×neurons]. A column of $W$ is one neuron’s weights, not a row.
levels.layer.hint2: Add $b$ [neurons] to $xW$: broadcasting gives every point the same biases.
levels.3-6.title: Draw a boundary
levels.3-6.description:
Learn a straight boundary between two classes. Weight matrix $W$ [2,2] and bias $b$ [2] are trainable parameters. A linear layer computes scores $xW + b$; Softmax turns them into probabilities. The engine compares labels using cross entropy. Reach loss below 0.15 and 100% accuracy in 80 steps; grading uses training samples, not a separate test set.
This level: input coordinates $x$ [40,2]; output $y$ [40,2] gives each point’s two class probabilities, not loss.
levels.3-6.hint1: Use a trainable linear layer to score both classes, then convert scores to probabilities. The learning rate controls update size.
levels.3-6.hint2: Use Parameter $W$ [2,2], $b$ [2] with Linear layer, then output Softmax. Try learning rate 0.1.
levels.3-7.title: Remember the last step
levels.3-7.description:
Momentum accumulates gradients into a velocity, speeding updates when directions agree. With current gradient $g$ and previous momentum $m$, compute $m′ = 0.9m + g$, then update weight using $w′ = w − 0.1m′$. This is one momentum step, not Adam.
This level: inputs are weight $w$, gradient $g$, old momentum $m$, all []; output $y$ [] is the new weight.
levels.3-7.hint1: Multiply the previous momentum $m$ by 0.9, then add the new gradient $g$.
levels.3-7.hint2: Multiply that new momentum by 0.1 and subtract it from $w$. The output is the updated parameter, not the momentum.
levels.3-8.title: Different scales, different steps
levels.3-8.description:
One small feature is useful; a large one is noise. A shared step size struggles to suit both. Adam adapts steps using each parameter’s gradient history; compare it with SGD. Reach loss below 0.15 and 100% accuracy in 600 steps. Grading uses training samples, with no separate test set.
This level: input features $x$ [40,2]; output $y$ [40,2] holds two class probabilities per sample.
levels.3-8.hint1:
Keep the model 
$$y = Softmax(xW + b)$$
, with $W$ [2×2] and $b$ [2]. The challenge is the update rule, not a bigger network.
levels.3-8.hint2: If one learning rate is too slow for one direction and too large for the other, try Adam. Reset parameters for a fair comparison.
levels.3-9.title: Bend the boundary
levels.3-9.description:
Concentric rings need more than a straight boundary. A hidden layer turns coordinates into new features; a nonlinear activation lets the second layer produce a curved decision region. $W₁$, $b₁$ are first-layer weights and biases; $W₂$, $b₂$ belong to the second. Without a nonlinear activation, both layers collapse to one linear transform plus bias.
The reference uses 16 Sigmoid hidden units. Reach loss below 0.15 and at least 95% accuracy in 300 steps. Grading uses training samples, with no separate test set.
This level: input coordinates $x$ [64,2]; output $y$ [64,2] gives each point’s two ring-class probabilities.
levels.3-9.hint1: Put a nonlinear activation between layers so hidden units form new features. Stacking linear layers alone is not enough.
levels.3-9.hint2: Reference: $W₁$ [2,16], $b₁$ [16] → Sigmoid → $W₂$ [16,2], $b₂$ [2] → Softmax. Initialize weights with Normal, scales 1 and 0.5 respectively; use zero biases and Adam at 0.05. Random weights break hidden-unit symmetry. You may also try 8 ReLU units; reset parameters and check loss and accuracy after 300 steps.
levels.train_accuracy: The step budget is exhausted. Loss is low enough, but accuracy is only {accuracy}, below the target.
levels.4-1.title: Characters to numbers
levels.4-1.description:
From this chapter on the network reads text. A circuit only computes with numbers, so each character first becomes an ID, say h → 0, e → 1, l → 2, o → 3.
An ID is a name, not a size: l is not “twice” e. So the network doesn’t use the ID itself; each character gets a row instead, one cell per kind of character, with 1 in its own ID’s cell and 0 elsewhere. This is one-hot encoding. With 5 kinds of characters:
$$2 ↦ [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]$$
This level: input idx is a run of character IDs, such as [0, 2, 4, 1]. Input k is every possible ID [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]; how many numbers it has is how many kinds of characters there are.
Output y: one row per character, one column per possible ID. Row i, column j is 1 exactly when the i-th ID in idx equals j. The expected y on the right labels its rows and columns, so you can compare.
levels.4-1.hint1: Row $i$, column $j$ answers “is the $i$-th ID equal to $j$?”. Use Insert dimension to make idx a column [4×1]; compared with $k$ [V] it broadcasts to a [4×V] table where each cell compares one pair.
levels.4-1.hint2: There is no “equals” part, but $a = b$ means “$a ≥ b$ and $b ≥ a$”. Greater or equal outputs 1 or 0; multiply the two results and only equal cells are 1.
levels.4-2.title: Look up a row
levels.4-2.description:
A vector gives each character a numerical representation for the network to learn from. Looking it up means selecting a row by character ID.
This level: idx holds 4 IDs [4]; table holds character vectors [5×3]. Output $y$ [4×3], with the selected rows in ID order. Tests vary both the table size and the number of IDs.
levels.4-2.hint1: For IDs [2,0], take rows 2 and 0 in that order, counting from zero. Why does multiplying a one-hot matrix by the table select exactly these rows?
levels.4-2.hint2: Use Dimension size with Axis set to 0 to read the row count from table. Feed it into Range length n on Range to get all IDs. Use those IDs and idx with One-hot, then Matrix multiply by table. Passing unlocks Embedding for direct lookups.
levels.4-3.title: The next character
levels.4-3.description:
Start with the simplest text prediction: given one character, guess the next. The corpus begins with little, giving pairs l→i, i→t, t→t, t→l and l→e. A character can have different successors, so the answer is a probability distribution, not a single choice.
After training, try continuing the text with “Write”. Training and grading use every adjacent pair in the corpus; cross entropy must be below about 2.181574. This does not show how well the model handles unseen text.
This level: $N$ is the number of pairs and $V$ the vocabulary size. Input $x$ [N] holds current-character IDs. Output $y$ [N×V] gives next-character probabilities, one row per pair.
levels.4-3.hint1: Let a Parameter table remember what tends to follow each character. Use shape [V×V]: rows represent current characters, columns represent possible next characters. Store scores, not probabilities yet.
levels.4-3.hint2: Use Gather: connect the parameter table to Table and $x$ to Indices. Turn each selected row of scores into probabilities with Softmax, then output them. Adam adjusts the scores using cross entropy; you can adjust the learning rate.
levels.4-4.title: Draw a character
levels.4-4.description:
Sample to vary the text.
This level: probabilities $p$ [5], random scalar $u$, cumulative-sum table triangle [5×5]; output one character ID (a scalar).
levels.4-4.hint1: $u$ lies between 0 and 1. Probabilities [0.2,0.5,0.3] divide that interval into three parts: $u = 0.6$ selects the second, ID 1. In triangle, the diagonal and cells above it are 1; the rest are 0. Use it to find the interval endpoints. Tests also use 8 characters.
levels.4-4.hint2: Use Insert dimension to make the probabilities a column, multiply by triangle, then Sum along axis 0. This gives cumulative probabilities, such as [0.2,0.7,1]. Compare the random number with each endpoint using Greater or equal, then Sum: the number of endpoints passed is the character ID.
levels.reshape.title: Reshape
levels.reshape.description:
The next model needs two character vectors together. Practise joining them into one row without mixing samples.
For example, one sample’s vectors [1,2,3] and [4,5,6] become [1,2,3,4,5,6]. Reshape changes grouping, not value order or count. Transpose instead swaps axes.
This level: $N$ is the sample count and $D$ the character-vector length. Input $x$ [N×2×D]; output $y$ [N×2D], one row per sample. The default [2×2×3] becomes [2×6]. Tests vary $N$ and $D$, so do not hard-code them.
levels.reshape.hint1: Reshape’s Shape can contain one −1, asking the part to infer that dimension from the total value count. This differs from axis −1 meaning the last axis. Which dimension must stay unchanged?
levels.reshape.hint2: Connect $x$ to Dimension size with Axis set to 0 to get $N$. Connect that to Reshape’s Target dimension 0 and set Shape to [1, −1]. The wire sets the first dimension; the second becomes $2D$ automatically.
levels.4-5.title: One more character
levels.4-5.description:
An extra character gives another clue. For example, th often precedes e, while sh can precede o. Give the network both characters to learn such patterns.
Training and grading use the same fixed 512 two-character samples. Cross entropy must be below about 1.639788; no unseen text is tested.
This level: input $x$ [512×2] holds two preceding character IDs per row. $V$ is the vocabulary size. Output $y$ [512×V] gives the next-character probabilities for each row.
levels.4-5.hint1: Let $D$ be the number of values representing a character. Create a Parameter table [V×D]. Gather the two vectors to get [512×2×D], then join each sample into a row [512×2D], as in the previous level.
levels.4-5.hint2: Use Matrix multiply plus a bias, then Tanh, so both characters influence a hidden layer. Project to $V$ candidate scores per row, then apply Softmax. The threshold is lower than the best result using only the last character: try learning combinations of both.
worker.generation_unavailable: This circuit cannot generate text. On a text-generation level, complete the circuit with the required output shape, then retry.
worker.invalid_probabilities: The output is not valid character probabilities: values must be finite and nonnegative, with a positive total. Check the final Softmax and run tests first.
ui.generateHelp: Uses the parameters from your latest training; untrained, it writes gibberish. Each step takes the context at the end of the existing text, runs a forward pass, samples one character from the last position's probabilities, appends it, and repeats. Generation does not update parameters. Low temperature plays safe, high takes chances.

errors.size_axis: Axis {actual} is out of range or not an integer: input rank is {rank}; available axes: {allowed}. Choose one of these; an empty list means no axis is available.
errors.dim_not_static: The length at input {port} must come from constants or input shapes, not changing data. Connect a Constant, or calculate the length from Dimension size.
errors.dim_not_integer: Length {actual} at input {port} is not a finite integer. Compute an integer length from constants or input shapes.
errors.dim_out_of_range: Input {port} sets axis {actual} (counting from 0), but target shape {shape} has only {rank} axes. Add a target dimension or disconnect this extra length input.
levels.5-1.title: Who should look at whom?
levels.5-1.description:
Attention scores measure relevance: query $q$ describes what to find, key $k$ what is available. $T$ counts positions and $D$ is vector width. Divide dot products by $√D$ to avoid overly sharp Softmax weights.
This level: queries $q$ and keys $k$ [T,D] → score table $y$ [T,T]; default [4,3] → [4,4]. A leading batch axis is also tested.
levels.5-1.hint1: Compare each query with every key to form one row of scores; obtain width from the input rather than fixing it. For query [1,0] and key [2,3], the dot product is 2, scaled to $2/√2$.
levels.5-1.hint2: Use Transpose on the last two key axes, then Matrix multiply. Dimension size gives $D$; apply Square root, then Divide the scores by it.
levels.5-2.title: Do not peek ahead
levels.5-2.description:
A causal mask prevents peeking at answers: row $i$ may read columns $j≤i$, including itself. $T$ counts positions. Keep entries on and below the diagonal; replace later entries with exactly -1e9 so Softmax gives them zero weight. Tests compare scores, not probabilities; $T$ varies.
This level: scores is a [T,T] score table; output $y$ is the masked table of the same shape, default [4,4]. A leading batch axis is also tested.
levels.5-2.hint1: Build the allowed region from row and column positions using Range, Insert dimension and Greater or equal. For example, row 1 can see columns 0 and 1, but not column 2; count from zero.
levels.5-2.hint2: Use Dimension size and Range to create position indices. Arrange row indices as [T,1] and column indices as [1,T]. Greater or equal gives mask $m$, with 1 where viewing is allowed. Keep the original scores multiplied by $m$; fill the other cells with −1 billion, not negative infinity.
levels.5-3.title: Mix the useful information
levels.5-3.description:
Attention mixes relevant content: $q$ is the query, $k$ the key and $v$ the value. Mask future positions, then Softmax each row into weights summing to 1. $T$ counts positions; key width $D$ and value width $E$ may differ, but their position counts must match.
This level: $q,k$ [T,D] and $v$ [T,E] → mixed content $y$ [T,E]; default all [4,3]. A leading batch axis is also tested.
levels.5-3.hint1: First decide where to look and how much, then mix values with those weights. Each position may read itself and earlier positions. For example, weights [0.25,0.75] mix values [2,6] to give $0.25×2+0.75×6=5$.
levels.5-3.hint2: Connect Scaled attention scores → Causal mask → Softmax on the last axis → Matrix multiply by $v$.
levels.5-4.title: Give each character a position
levels.5-4.description:
Add position vectors to character vectors so the same character can differ by position.
This level: idx holds character IDs [4], tokens is the token table [7,3], positions the position table [8,3]; $y$ holds position-aware vectors [4,3]. Tests vary shapes and may batch idx.
levels.5-4.hint1: Look up characters and positions separately; generate position IDs from sequence length, not character IDs. For example, the same character vector [2,3] plus position [1,0] or [0,1] becomes [3,3] or [2,4].
levels.5-4.hint2: Use Dimension size on the last idx axis, then Range for position IDs. Gather from each table and Add; position vectors broadcast across batches.
levels.5-5.title: Learn with attention
levels.5-5.description:
Train attention to predict the next character: $q$ is the query, $k$ the key, and $v$ the content to carry. Obtain them through separate projections of the same token-plus-position vectors. Project Attention outputs to vocabulary scores, then use Softmax for probabilities.
Each window contains 9 characters: the first 8 are inputs and the last 8 are targets shifted one place ahead. Position $i$ reads only itself and earlier inputs to predict character $i+1$. Training practices all 8 positions in parallel; it does not generate 8 new characters at once. Generation samples one character, appends it, then runs again.
Train with Adam for 200 steps. Training and grading use the same 128 fixed windows; cross entropy averaged over all positions must be below 1.75. This is not an independent unseen-text test.
This level: $x$ holds character IDs [128,8]; $y$ gives next-character probabilities at each position [128,8,27], with a vocabulary of 27 characters.
levels.5-5.hint1: Start with Token + position embedding. Use three separate Parameter projections for queries, keys and values, then Attention. Their roles emerge from the prediction loss. For example, window little mo gives input little m and target ittle mo: each position predicts its successor.
levels.5-5.hint2: Use token table [27,12], position table [8,12], three projections [12,12] and output projection [12,27]; finish with Softmax.
levels.6-1.title: Look in several ways at once
levels.6-1.description:
Multi-head attention lets channel groups choose independently where to look. $B$ counts batches, $T$ positions, and $D$ channels (vector components at each position). Split into two heads, each using $D/2$ channels for causal attention, then merge in the original order. What heads attend to is learned, not assigned by hand. Obtain sizes from inputs rather than fixing them.
This level: queries $q$, keys $k$ and values $v$ all have shape [B,T,D]; output $y$ holds merged content with that same shape, default [2,4,8].
levels.6-1.hint1: Split channels, apply Attention independently across positions in each head, then merge. Do not attend across heads. For example, four channels [1,2,3,4] split into heads [1,2] and [3,4], each comparing positions separately.
levels.6-1.hint2: Reshape to [B,T,2,D/2], then Transpose the middle axes. Apply Attention, swap back and merge. Divide each head’s scores by $√(D/2)$; projections belong outside this component.
levels.6-2.title: Think at each position
levels.6-2.description:
Feed-forward network processes each position independently with shared weights: widen, apply ReLU, then narrow. $B,T,D,H$ denote batch, positions, input width and hidden width.
This level: vectors $x$ [B,T,D], weights w1 [D,H], w2 [H,D], biases b1 [H], b2 [D] → processed vectors $y$ [B,T,D]. Defaults: B=2,T=4,D=8,H=16.
levels.6-2.hint1: Widen and activate, then narrow; share weights and biases without mixing positions. For example, width 2 can expand to 4 and shrink back to 2; the number of positions stays unchanged.
levels.6-2.hint2: Use Matrix multiply and Add twice: multiply $x$ by w1, add b1, then apply ReLU. Multiply that by w2 and add b2. Biases broadcast across batches and positions.
levels.6-3.title: Build a Transformer block
levels.6-3.description:
A Transformer block exchanges information between positions, then processes each position. Normalize before each branch and add its result to its input (a residual).
This level: vectors $x$ [B,T,D]; attention weights wq/wk/wv/wo each [D,D]; feed-forward weights w1 [D,H], w2 [H,D], biases b1 [H], b2 [D] → updated vectors $y$ [B,T,D]. B/T/D/H mean batch/positions/channels/hidden width, default 2/4/8/16.
levels.6-3.hint1: Use Layer normalization before each branch, then add its result to the original branch input. Residuals preserve information and a direct gradient path; do not normalize after the addition instead. For example, adding branch result [0.1,−0.2] to input [1,2] gives [1.1,1.8].
levels.6-3.hint2: Normalize $x$, project with wq/wk/wv, use Multi-head attention, multiply by wo and add $x$ to get $h$. Apply Layer normalization to $h$, then Feed-forward network with w1/b1/w2/b2; add the result to $h$ for $y$.
levels.6-4.title: Let your Transformer write
levels.6-4.description:
Build a small GPT predictor: token-plus-position vectors → two Transformer blocks → Layer normalization → vocabulary projection → Softmax. Each block uses independent trainable parameters; causal attention prevents peeking ahead.
Train with Adam for 1500 steps, sampling 8 windows per step. Every 250 steps and at the end, evaluate without updates on 400 fixed windows from the same corpus. Their mean cross entropy must be below 1.1. Passing does not use the last minibatch loss or an independent test set; low loss guarantees neither fluent generation nor good predictions on new text.
Generation samples one character from the last position, appends it and runs again using trained weights without updating them.
This level: $x$ holds character IDs, [8,16] for training and [400,16] for evaluation. Output $y$ gives next-character probabilities at each position, respectively [8,16,27] and [400,16,27]; the vocabulary has 27 characters.
levels.6-4.hint1: Start with Token + position embedding and two Transformer block components. Give each block independent attention and feed-forward parameters; keep channel widths aligned. For example, after reading little, draw just one character. If it is a space, the next prediction uses little followed by that space.
levels.6-4.hint2: Use token table [27,24], position table [16,24], channel width 24 and hidden width 48 per block. Finish with Layer normalization, a [24,27] Parameter projection and Softmax.
loop.title: The training loop: five things, every step
loop.data.name: Take a batch
loop.data.fixed: The same samples every step, computed together (3-6)
loop.data.resample: A fresh random batch from the corpus every step
loop.forward.name: Forward
loop.forward.note: Compute predictions with current parameters. The level supplies data and answers; you choose wiring and parameter shapes. Training changes parameter values, not wiring or answers.
loop.loss.name: Loss
loop.loss.note: Compare predictions with answers for this step’s training batch to get a smaller-is-better number (3-5 MSE, 3-7 cross entropy). The level explains which data are graded and the loss threshold; classification levels also require accuracy.
loop.backward.name: Backward
loop.backward.note: The chain rule gives every parameter its gradient; you did it by hand in 3-1 and 3-2, now the engine does it
loop.update.name: Update
loop.update.sgd: Each parameter takes a small step against its gradient: w ← w − {lr}·gradient (3-1)
loop.update.adam: Adam: each parameter sizes its own step from its history, base step {lr} (3-9, 3-10)
loop.repeat: Return to step 1, {steps} times in all. Lower loss means better predictions on the measured data, not necessarily on new data. Memorizing training data without handling new data is called overfitting.
coach.title: Getting started
coach.mul: This level asks for −x. The idea: multiply x by −1. First drag "Multiply" from the parts on the left onto the canvas (a click works too).
coach.wireX: Inputs are on a part's left, outputs on its right. Press on the square to the right of x, drag it to the a port on the left of Multiply, and let go.
coach.const: Now add a "Constant" and wire it to Multiply's b port. Select it and set its value to −1 under Properties on the right.
coach.wireY: Finally wire Multiply's output to y. The live values on the right then show y; compare it with "Expected" below it.
coach.run: If they match, press "Run tests" on the right: the engine checks your circuit on many values of x. Pass them all and the part is yours.
training.nonfinite.hint.log: Logarithm needs a strictly positive input. Inspect the value on its incoming wire.
training.nonfinite.hint.exp: Exponential overflows for large inputs. Reduce them; for Softmax, subtract each row’s maximum first.
training.nonfinite.hint.div: Division needs a nonzero denominator; tiny denominators can also produce huge results. Inspect its denominator wire.
training.nonfinite.hint.recip: Reciprocal cannot take zero; tiny inputs can also produce huge results. If built using Logarithm, its input must also be positive.
training.nonfinite.hint.sqrt: Square root needs nonnegative input; a construction using Logarithm needs strictly positive input. Inspect the input wire.
training.nonfinite.hint.param: Check this parameter’s initial value. Excessive learning rates can make parameters diverge; lower the rate and reset training.
training.nonfinite.hint.default: Inspect values along the input wires. If initial values are valid but training later fails, lower the learning rate and restart training.
training.nonfinite.value: Output value {index} of this part is {actual}.
levels.4-1.expectedNote: Each row is one character (its ID on the left); each column is one possible ID (the number from k on top). A row has its 1 in the column of its ID.
levels.2-4.expectedNote: Each cell multiplies its row and column values.
levels.2-5.expectedNote: Each cell dots a left row with a right column.
levels.2-6.expectedNote: Each cell dots a left row with a right row.
levels.layer.expectedNote: Rows are samples; columns are neurons, from 0.
levels.4-2.expectedNote: Each row holds the vector for its labeled ID.
levels.5-1.expectedNote: Rows query keys in columns; positions start at 0.
levels.5-2.expectedNote: Rows query keys; future positions are blocked.
levels.5-3.expectedNote: Each query row holds a weighted value vector.
levels.5-4.expectedNote: Rows show position:ID and sum both vectors.
